1.text_clean:
1. A ball of mass 2.7 g is released from rest from a height of 28 m above horizontal ground.
[Diagram: ball at height 28 m above horizontal ground]
(a) Show that in the absence of air resistance the ball impacts the ground with a speed of about 23 m s$^{-1}$. [1]
(b) An air resistance force $F$ acts on the ball. $F$ can be modeled by $F = kv^2$ where $v$ is the speed and $k$ is a constant.
(i) Determine the unit of $k$ in terms of fundamental units. [2]
(ii) Describe how the ball reaches terminal speed. [2]
(c) The graph shows the variation with time $t$ of the speed $v$ of the ball from the instant it is released until it impacts the ground.
[Graph: v / m s$^{-1}$ (0 to 10) against t / s (0 to 4); curve rises from origin, roughly linearly at first, then levels off at about 9.5 m s$^{-1}$, ending at about t = 3.6 s]
(i) State the value of the area under the curve. [1]
(ii) Determine $k$. [2]
(iii) On the axes below, draw a graph to show the variation of the magnitude of the resultant force, $F$, on the ball with time $t$. No numbers are required on the axes. [1]
[Blank axes: F against t, origin 0]
(iv) Calculate the average power dissipated by the air resistance force. [3]
(d) The ball rebounds from the ground with speed 7.8 m s$^{-1}$. The ball is in contact with the ground for a time $T$. The average resultant force on the ball during this time is 1.1 N.
Determine $T$. [2]

2.text_clean:
2. Crushed ice of mass 35 g at temperature $-10$ °C is placed in a warm room. The graph shows the variation of the temperature $T$ of the ice with time $t$.
[Graph: T / °C (−10 to 5) against t / min (0 to 70); temperature rises linearly from −10 °C at t = 0 to 0 °C at t = 4 min, then stays at 0 °C until about t = 64 min]
The specific heat capacity of ice is 2100 J kg$^{-1}$ K$^{-1}$.
(a) (i) Show that the average rate at which thermal energy is being transferred into the ice is about 3 W. [2]
(ii) Estimate the specific latent heat of fusion of ice. [2]
(b) Between 4 minutes and 64 minutes solid ice and liquid water coexist at 0 °C. Compare and contrast, during this time, the internal energy of solid ice to that of an equal mass of liquid water. [2]

3.text_clean:
3. (a) Outline what is meant by a travelling wave. [2]
(b) A loudspeaker emits sound of frequency 210 Hz into a pipe with one open and one closed end. The diagram shows a representation of the standing wave established in the pipe.
[Diagram: pipe closed at left end, open at right end, loudspeaker at right; standing wave pattern showing three-quarters of a wavelength (node at closed end, antinode at open end)]
The length of the pipe is 1.20 m.
(i) Outline how the standing wave is formed in the pipe. [2]
(ii) Determine the wavelength of the wave. [1]
(iii) Calculate the speed of sound in the pipe stating the answer to an appropriate number of significant figures. [2]
(c) The solid line represents the standing wave at time $t$ and the dotted line represents the standing wave at an instant later. The dot is the equilibrium position of a particle P in the pipe. The up arrow indicates displacements to the right and the down arrow displacements to the left.
[Diagram: pipe with solid and dotted standing-wave curves; particle P equilibrium position marked as a dot near the left end; vertical double arrow at the left indicating displacement direction]
On the diagram, draw
(i) a dot to indicate the approximate position of P at time $t$, [1]
(ii) an arrow to indicate the velocity of P at time $t$. [1]
(d) The amplitude of oscillations of the standing wave in (b) is 4.2 mm. The mass of particle P in (c) is $1.8 \times 10^{-6}$ kg.
Calculate
(i) the total energy of P, [2]
(ii) the displacement of P, when its kinetic energy is equal to its potential energy. [2]
(e) The frequency of sound is reduced to 140 Hz. Explain why a standing wave will not be formed in the pipe. [2]

4.text_clean:
4. (a) The diagram shows a junction in a circuit.
[Diagram: current $I_1$ flows into a junction; currents $I_2$ and $I_3$ flow out along two branches]
The currents in the three wires are related by $I_1 = I_2 + I_3$.
State the fundamental law of Physics from which this relation is derived. [1]
(b) A cell of emf 1.50 V and internal resistance $r$ is connected to a resistor of resistance 5.00 Ω and an ideal voltmeter V.
[Circuit: cell (1.50 V, internal resistance r) with voltmeter V and a 5.00 Ω resistor connected in parallel across it]
The reading of the voltmeter is 1.20 V.
(i) Determine the internal resistance $r$ of the cell. [2]
(ii) A second 5.00 Ω resistor is connected in parallel to the first resistor.
[Circuit: as before with two 5.00 Ω resistors in parallel]
State and explain the change, if any, in the voltmeter reading without further calculation. [2]
(c) A proton moves on a circular path in a region of uniform magnetic field of magnetic flux density $B$ that is directed into the plane of the page.
[Diagram: field into page (crosses); proton on the leftmost point of a dashed circular path]
(i) On the diagram, draw an arrow to indicate the velocity of the proton at the position shown. [1]
(ii) Show that the frequency of revolution of the proton is given by $f = \frac{eB}{2\pi m_p}$. [3]
(iii) The magnitude of $B$ is 2.5 T. Calculate the frequency of revolution of the proton. [1]

5.text_clean:
5. A probe of mass $m$ has landed on the equator of a rotating asteroid of mass $M$ and radius $R$.
[Diagram (not to scale): asteroid of mass M and radius R rotating about a vertical axis; probe of mass m on its equator]
The asteroid rotates with angular speed $\omega$.
(a) By drawing a free-body diagram for the probe, show that the normal force, $N$, on the probe from the asteroid is given by $N = m\left(\frac{GM}{R^2} - \omega^2 R\right)$. [2]
[Box: probe m for free-body diagram]
(b) Deduce that the probe will remain on the asteroid surface only if $\omega \le \sqrt{\frac{GM}{R^3}}$. [1]
(c) Another probe orbits the Sun.
(i) The distance between the probe and the Sun is 4 times the distance between the Earth and the Sun. Show that the intensity of the solar radiation at the surface of the probe is 85 W m$^{-2}$. [2]
(ii) Estimate the equilibrium temperature of the probe assuming it behaves as a black body. [2]
5.note: c(i) solar constant/inverse-square tagged B.2; could be B.1 | audit: inverse-square intensity + black-body temperature (3 marks) are B.1; solar constant 1 mark B.2

6.text_clean:
6. (a) Quarks are elementary particles.
(i) State what is meant by an elementary particle. [1]
(ii) List the fundamental forces that act on quarks. [1]
(iii) The lambda baryon ($\Lambda^0$) has quark content uds. It decays according to the reaction $\Lambda^0 \to p + \pi^-$. The quark content of the pion is $\bar{u}d$.
State and explain which fundamental interaction is responsible for this decay. [2]
(b) (i) By reference to the concept of binding energy, explain why the combined mass of the nucleons of a nucleus is greater than the mass of the nucleus. [2]
(ii) The following binding energies per nucleon are available:
Th: 7.645074 MeV
Ra: 7.679917 MeV
He: 7.073915 MeV
Determine the energy released in the decay ${}^{228}_{90}\mathrm{Th} \to {}^{224}_{88}\mathrm{Ra} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$. [2]
(iii) It is observed that, sometimes, the alpha decay of thorium is accompanied by gamma ray emission. Suggest an explanation for this observation. [2]

7.text_clean:
7. Light of wavelength $\lambda$ diffracts at a single rectangular slit of opening $b$. The diagram shows two rays of light leaving the top and middle of the slit. The rays come from the same wavefront. The angle of diffraction is $\theta$. For small angles the approximation $\sin\theta \approx \theta$ may be used.
[Diagram (not to scale): plane wave incident on slit of width b; rays from top and middle of slit at angle θ meet at point P on a distant screen]
The rays meet at point P on a screen a very large distance from the slit.
(a) (i) Show that the phase difference between the two rays at P is $\frac{\pi b\theta}{\lambda}$. [2]
(ii) The two rays interfere destructively at P to form the first minimum of the single slit diffraction pattern. Explain why $\theta = \frac{\lambda}{b}$. [1]
(b) The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has an effective diameter of 6.5 m.
(i) Calculate the smallest linear size at a distance of 13.6 billion light years ($1.3 \times 10^{26}$ m) that can be resolved by the JWST when it operates at a wavelength of 1200 nm. [2]
(ii) The JWST can also operate at wavelengths longer than 1200 nm. Suggest whether the resolution of the telescope is improved at the longer wavelengths. [1]

8.text_clean:
8. A uniform, spherical planet P has mass $M$ and radius $R$.
(a) A projectile of mass $m$ is launched with kinetic energy $\frac{2GMm}{3R}$ from the surface of P.
[Diagram (not to scale): planet P with projectile launched radially outward from its surface]
Determine whether the projectile will escape the gravitational field of P. [2]
(b) The surface of P is an equipotential surface $E_0$. The dotted circle labeled $E_1$ is an equipotential line at a distance $\frac{3R}{2}$ from the centre of P. The potential difference between $E_1$ and $E_0$ is $2.2 \times 10^6$ J kg$^{-1}$.
[Diagram: grid with planet P (surface E0) and dashed concentric circle E1 of radius 3R/2]
(i) The radius $R$ of P is $8.5 \times 10^6$ m.
Estimate the magnitude of the gravitational field strength between $E_1$ and $E_0$. [2]
(ii) $E_2$ is an equipotential line such that the potential difference between $E_2$ and $E_1$ is also $2.2 \times 10^6$ J kg$^{-1}$.
Draw the equipotential line $E_2$ on the diagram. [2]

9. (a) A conducting rod of length $L$ is moved with speed $v$ at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of flux density $B$. The field is directed into the plane of the page.
[Diagram: horizontal rod of length L moving downward with speed v in a magnetic field B directed into the page]
(i) Show, using Faraday's law or otherwise, that the potential difference, $V$, established between the ends of the rod is $V = vBL$. [3]
(ii) Identify the end of the rod that becomes negatively charged. [1]
(b) A coil is rotating in a region of magnetic field with angular speed 12.56 rad s$^{-1}$. At $t = 0$, the field is parallel to the surface of the coil.
[Diagram: rectangular coil rotating about an axis in a uniform horizontal field B, plane of coil parallel to field]
(i) State the magnetic flux linkage through the coil at $t = 0$. [1]
(ii) Draw, on the axes, a graph to show the variation with time of the induced emf in the loop. (No numbers are required on the vertical axis.) [2]
[Blank axes: emf against time / s from 0 to 1, marked 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1]
(c) A capacitor is connected to a cell. The switch S is closed and the capacitor becomes fully charged.
[Circuit: capacitor in series with a cell and switch S]
A dielectric is then inserted in between the plates of the capacitor. Suggest what, if anything, will happen to the charge on one plate of the capacitor. [2]

10.text_clean:
10. (a) (i) In the Bohr model for the hydrogen atom orbital angular momentum is quantized ($mvr = n\frac{h}{2\pi}$). Outline the effect this has on the electron energy. [1]
(ii) For the hydrogen atom, the orbit radius of the electron in the $n = 2$ state is four times larger than the orbit radius in the $n = 1$ state. Determine the ratio $\frac{v_2}{v_1}$ of the electron speed in the $n = 2$ state to the speed in the $n = 1$. [2]
(b) Compare and contrast the Bohr prediction for the radius of an electron orbit in hydrogen to that of the description of the electron in terms of a wave function. [2]
(c) Determine, using the uncertainty principle, the minimum kinetic energy of a neutron inside a nucleus of radius $3 \times 10^{-15}$ m. [2]
